🚨 WHAT IF YOUR CHILD’S THERAPY ISN’T THE WHOLE STORY?

Speech therapy.
OT.
Special education.
Behaviour therapy.
Home programs.

Parents are doing EVERYTHING.

And yet sometimes you think:

“Why isn’t my child progressing the way I expected?”

Here’s the mindset shift I want every parent to hear:

👉 Therapy happens in a body.

If your child is struggling with constipation, reflux, poor sleep, nutritional gaps, chronic discomfort, sensory overload, stress or an extremely limited diet, they may have a much harder time being available for learning.

A child who didn't sleep well may struggle to attend.

A child with physical discomfort may communicate through behaviour.

A child who is constantly overwhelmed may have very little capacity left for interaction.

A child surviving on a tiny range of foods may need their nutrition looked at—not blamed or ignored.

This does NOT mean:

❌ “Gut problems cause autism.”
❌ “Detox will cure your child.”
❌ “Stop therapy.”
❌ “You need 47 supplements.”

It means we stop looking at the child through ONE window.

🧠 Brain
🗣️ Communication
🦴 Movement
👂 Sensory system
😴 Sleep
🥗 Nutrition
💩 Digestion
❤️ Emotional regulation
🏠 Home environment

All of these can influence how a child feels and functions during the day.

Your child doesn't need to spend every waking hour inside therapy rooms.

The real work also happens in the other 23 hours.

At the dining table.
During bedtime.
In the bathroom.
While playing.
During transitions.
When they are upset.
When they are communicating without words.

✨ Therapy teaches skills.
Daily life gives those skills a place to grow.

So don't just ask:

“Which therapy should I add next?”

Start asking:

“What is my child’s body, behaviour and environment trying to tell me?”

Because sometimes the missing piece isn't MORE therapy.

Sometimes it's understanding the child BETTER. ❤️

👀 WHY DOES MY AUTISTIC CHILD WATCH THEIR FINGERS MOVE?

That little finger movement may look unusual to us…

But for your child, the movement itself may be fascinating. 💙

When an autistic child watches their fingers move in front of their eyes, they may be experiencing:

✨ VISUAL STIMULATION — enjoying the movement, shadows, light, or changing patterns.

🔄 PREDICTABILITY — repeating the same movement creates something familiar and predictable.

🌿 SELF-REGULATION — repetitive movements may help some children organize their sensory experience or feel more settled.

😊 PURE ENJOYMENT — sometimes, it simply feels interesting or satisfying.

👀 SENSORY EXPLORATION — your child may be exploring how movement, vision, and attention work together.

And here’s the important part:

There isn't one single reason behind this behavior.

The same behavior can serve completely different purposes for different children.

So instead of immediately asking…

❌ “How do I stop this?”

Try asking:

💙 “What is my child experiencing right now?”

Observe the pattern:

• When does it happen?
• What happens just before it?
• What happens afterward?
• Is your child happy, excited, focused, tired, or overwhelmed?
• Does the movement help them settle or engage?

When we understand the function behind a behavior, we can respond with curiosity rather than immediately trying to eliminate it.

Because sometimes, what looks like “just a repetitive movement” is actually your child's way of exploring, enjoying, communicating, or regulating their world. 💙

📌 DISCLAIMER: This post is for general educational purposes only and is not a diagnostic or individualized recommendation. Repetitive or sensory behaviors can have different functions for different autistic people. If a behavior causes injury, significant distress, or substantially interferes with daily life, seek individualized guidance from an appropriately qualified professional.

🧩 EVERY TINY SUCCESS IS DATA.

Your autistic child tried something today that they couldn’t do yesterday.

Maybe they: ✨ looked toward you for one second
✨ used a word instead of pulling your hand
✨ tolerated a new texture
✨ waited for their turn
✨ stayed with an activity for 30 seconds longer
✨ came back after getting frustrated
✨ attempted something independently

You may think, “It’s such a small thing.”

But your child’s brain may be learning something much bigger:

“Oh… maybe I CAN do this.” 💛

Every successful attempt gives the brain new information.

It starts challenging the old prediction: ❌ “I can’t.” ❌ “This is too difficult.” ❌ “I always need someone to do it for me.”

And slowly creates a new one:

✅ “I tried.” ✅ “I managed.” ✅ “I can try again.” ✅ “Maybe I CAN do this.”

That tiny moment of success matters.

So parents, don't measure your child's progress only by milestones or comparisons.

Look for the tiny evidence of growth.

Because sometimes transformation doesn't begin with a huge breakthrough.

It begins with one tiny success repeated again and again. 🌱

🫧 TEACH YOUR PRESCHOOLER ABOUT THEIR “BUBBLE OF CONSENT” 🫧

Every child has an invisible bubble around their body.
That bubble belongs to THEM. 

Teach your child:

🫧 “This is my bubble.”
I decide who can come close.

✋ “Stop means STOP.”
If I don't want a hug, kiss, tickle or touch, I can say NO.

🙅‍♀️ “My body belongs to me.”
Even adults and people I love should ask before touching my body.

💬 “I can say NO politely—or loudly if I need to.”

🏃‍♀️ “I can move away.”
I don't have to stay near someone who makes me uncomfortable.

👩‍👧 “I can always tell a safe adult.”
And I will not get into trouble for telling.

Make it a daily game:

Ask your child:
“Can I enter your bubble?”

Wait for their answer.

If they say YES → come closer.
If they say NO → respect it immediately.

Then reverse roles:
“Can I come into Mama/Papa's bubble?”

This teaches children that consent is not just a safety lesson—it is a two-way habit of respecting boundaries. 🌈

❤️ Remember: Don't force children to hug, kiss or sit with relatives just to be “polite.” Teach them that kindness and consent can exist together.

Start the bubble game today. 🫧

I’d start making small changes in our everyday routines — because language learning happens during ordinary moments too. ❤️

🌿 1. Give choices
Instead of asking an open-ended question, give two simple options:
“Do you want banana or apple?” 🍌🍎
This gives your child a reason to communicate, even if they’re only pointing or gesturing at first.

🌿 2. Comment more, question less
Rather than constantly asking, “What is that?”
Try narrating what’s happening:
“Wow, the car is going fast!” 🚗
“You’re putting the blocks on top!” 🧱

Your child gets to hear useful language without feeling like they’re being tested.

🌿 3. Create predictable verbal routines
Use the same short words or phrases during familiar activities.
Before meals: “Time to eat!”
Before leaving: “Bag on, let’s go!” 🎒
During bedtime: “Lights off, goodnight!” 🌙

Repetition makes language more predictable and easier to understand and eventually imitate.

And remember — **communication is not only spoken words.** Pointing, gestures, sounds, eye contact and attempts to interact all matter.

Is omega-3 really a “brain booster” for children? 🧠

You may have heard that DHA can make children smarter, improve memory, increase attention or even fix developmental challenges.

But the science is more nuanced.

DHA is one of the important omega-3 fatty acids found in high concentrations in the brain and retina. It becomes part of neuronal cell membranes and contributes to the environment in which brain cells communicate.

Think of it as part of the foundation—not a magic switch.

A child's brain development depends on much more than one nutrient:

✨ Nutrition
✨ Sleep
✨ Movement
✨ Learning opportunities
✨ Emotional connection
✨ Sensory experiences
✨ Overall health

And when it comes to omega-3, the source matters too.

Fish can provide DHA and EPA, while foods like chia seeds, flaxseeds and walnuts provide ALA. For vegetarian children with limited dietary DHA, algae-derived DHA may be something to discuss with a healthcare professional.

Most importantly, not every child automatically needs an omega-3 supplement.

Start by looking at the child's overall diet.

🎯 Is your child struggling to focus? Try these 5 simple exercises!

Instead of repeatedly saying “Focus karo!”, train the brain through play. 🧠✨

1️⃣ Freeze & Go – Say “Go!” and “Freeze!” to build listening and impulse control.

2️⃣ Spot the Difference – Give 2 similar pictures and ask your child to find 3–5 differences.

3️⃣ Balloon Tap – Keep a balloon in the air using only one hand. Great for visual attention + coordination.

4️⃣ Pattern Copying – Make a simple block/bead pattern and ask your child to copy it.

5️⃣ 1-Minute Listening Game – Ask your child to listen quietly and identify 3 sounds around them.

💡 Start with just 5–10 minutes daily.
Consistency matters more than long practice sessions.

Every milestone is precious, and parents eagerly wait to celebrate these special moments with family and friends.

Each month, your baby develops new skills that become the building blocks for communication, learning, movement, and social connection. While every child develops at their own pace, persistent delays or developmental differences deserve attention—not panic.

Early signs that may need attention:

👀 Limited or inconsistent eye contact
👂 Little or no response to sounds or their name
😊 Rarely smiles or shows limited social engagement
🙂 Limited facial expressions
🤲 Limited gestures or non-verbal communication
🧸 Limited interest in people or interactive play
🔄 Delays in rolling, sitting, or other motor milestones
👁️ Difficulty tracking moving objects
💬 Limited attempts to communicate through sounds, gestures, or expressions

Remember: One sign alone does not mean autism. Every child is unique. But if you notice multiple concerns or feel that something is different, don’t ignore your instincts.

❌ Gut serotonin does NOT simply travel to the brain.

❌ Probiotics do NOT “cure” autism.
❌ Essential oils do NOT reliably increase brain serotonin.

Instead, we need to look at the bigger picture:

✨ Digestion
✨ Bowel regularity
✨ Nutrition
✨ Sleep
✨ Sensory needs
✨ Communication
✨ Emotional regulation
✨ Medical concerns

Your child isn't always giving you a behavior problem.

Sometimes they're showing you a support problem.

The homework isn't getting done.

They're constantly moving.

They're shouting over tiny things.

They refuse to transition.

They seem to know what they should do—but still can't seem to start.

Before asking:

❌ “Why won't you listen?”

Try asking:

“What does my child need right now?”

Maybe it's:

→ A smaller task
→ A movement break
→ Less stimulation
→ A snack or water
→ Rest
→ Help getting started
→ Fewer instructions
→ A pause before trying again

That's why I created this simple ADHD Parent Decision Tree:

STOP → OBSERVE → CHECK → REGULATE → SIMPLIFY → SUPPORT → TRY AGAIN

It doesn't mean removing boundaries.

It means learning to respond to the need while still holding the boundary.

Because the goal isn't a perfectly behaved child.

The goal is a child who gradually learns:

“I can understand what is happening inside me. I can ask for help. I can try again.”
